summary: Gives a roadmap to the BGP-4 documents and reports on implementation experience, building on earlier BGP versions and their use in the connected Internet. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 1773.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1656 introduces BGP-4's purpose and summarizes early implementation experience. It describes support for classless routes and records practical concerns about aggregation and older protocol versions.

subtitle: A guide to BGP-4 documents and a report on early implementation experience.

tldr.problem: Readers needed context for BGP-4 and information about how its new classless routing mechanisms worked in implementations.
tldr.mechanism: The memo summarizes BGP-4's role and reports implementation and testing observations, including route aggregation and version negotiation concerns.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1656 is informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 1773.

facts.label: Route exchange
facts.value: All implementations could exchange reachability information

sections.title: What BGP-4 Does
sections.content:
Border Gateway Protocol version 4 (BGP-4) exchanges network reachability information between Autonomous Systems (ASs). The information includes the sequence of ASs through which a route passes, which can help identify routing loops and support policy decisions between ASs.

BGP-4 supports classless inter-domain routing by advertising IP prefixes without relying on network classes. It also adds mechanisms for aggregating routes and AS paths. It is designed for communication between ASs, not as a replacement for interior gateway protocols such as OSPF or RIP.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP-4 lets separate networks exchange information about which IP networks they can reach. It can describe routes without fixed address classes and can combine routes.

sections.title: Implementations and Testing
sections.content:
At the time of the memo, four vendors had developed independent implementations: ANS, Europanet, 3COM, and Cisco. The RFC reports extensive testing of one implementation in a network designed to mirror complex Internet borders, with routing information from several networks and additional AS adjacencies simulated using IP-over-IP tunnels.

The testing covered classless prefixes, route aggregation including AS sets, policy decisions based on AS sets, and features such as LOCAL_PREF and route-fluctuation damping. The memo does not claim that every implementation supported every feature.
sections.plainLanguage: Four vendors had independent BGP-4 implementations. Testing of one implementation exercised routes, aggregation, and several added features in a complex simulated network.

sections.title: Interoperability and Risks
sections.content:
All implementations could exchange reachability information, but not all could generate aggregate routes from more-specific routes. The memo says no implementation supported automatic deaggregation; some allowed controlled, static deaggregation for limited backward compatibility.

The RFC warns that deaggregation can cause a routing information explosion unless controlled. It also warns against automatic negotiation to older BGP versions: packet loss or restarts could result in a connection that cannot carry supernet, subnet, or AS-set information.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations could exchange routes, but their aggregation abilities differed. The memo warns that uncontrolled route expansion and automatic fallback to older versions can lose important routing information.
